Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: extract from Act 1, Scene 4 of Macbeth by William Shakespeare.

[DUNCAN has just named his son Malcolm heir to the throne, as Prince of Cumberland.]
MACBETH [Aside]: The Prince of Cumberland! That is a step
On which I must fall down, or else o'erleap,
For in my way it lies. Stars, hide your fires;
Let not light see my black and deep desires:
The eye wink at the hand; yet let that be
Which the eye fears, when it is done, to see.

How does Shakespeare use the aside to reveal Macbeth's ambition?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: Because it is an aside, Macbeth's thoughts are shared only with the audience, creating dramatic irony as Duncan continues to trust him. The metaphor of Malcolm as a "step" he must "o'erleap" shows his ambition – his hamartia – turning towards murder. His apostrophe "Stars, hide your fires" and the imagery of "black and deep desires" link ambition with darkness, while the rhyming couplet seals his dark resolve.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Because it is an aside, Macbeth's thoughts are shared only with the audience, creating dramatic irony as Duncan continues to trust him. The metaphor of Malcolm as a "step" he must "o'erleap" shows his ambition – his hamartia – turning towards murder. His apostrophe "Stars, hide your fires" and the imagery of "black and deep desires" link ambition with darkness, while the rhyming couplet seals his dark resolve. Criterion A (scaled to 5): 5 perceptive analysis of several choices with precise evidence; 3-4 substantial; 2 adequate; 1 limited.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text B: news report from a community news website.

FAMILIES FACE EVICTION AS COUNCIL BACKS £300M STADIUM
One hundred and forty families on the Riverside estate could lose their homes after councillors voted last night to build a stadium on the site.
"My children were born in this flat," said Joan Mensah, 62, who has lived on the estate for thirty years. "Nobody asked us."
The council claims the project will create 2,000 jobs. Campaigners say most will be temporary.

How does this report present the stadium decision?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The headline frames the story negatively, foregrounding "EVICTION" and families. The emotive quotation from Joan Mensah ("My children were born in this flat") turns a number into a human story, and "Nobody asked us" suggests injustice. The council's jobs figure is introduced with the distancing verb "claims" and immediately challenged by campaigners, who get the last word. Through framing, selection and order, the report favours residents.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: extract from a personal essay by a young writer.

For most of my life, my name has been the hardest word I know.
"Th-" I would begin, and the room would wait, and the wait would fill with kind faces trying not to look kind. Teachers finished my sentences. Friends ordered for me.
At fifteen I joined the debate club, mostly by accident. The first time I spoke, I stammered for eleven seconds – I know, because someone timed it.
Then I finished my argument. We won.
I still stammer. I have simply stopped apologising for the time it takes me to be heard.

Text B: speech by a candidate for school captain to a Year 10 assembly.

Good morning, Year 10. I'm not going to promise you a swimming pool, a four-day week or free pizza on Fridays. (I asked. The answer was no.)
What I will promise is this: a student council that actually meets, a suggestion box that someone actually opens, and a captain who actually listens.
Last year, ninety of us signed the petition for water fountains on the top floor. Nothing happened. This year, let's make something happen.
Vote Amira. Because "actually" is a promise I can keep.

Compare how the two writers present the challenge of speaking to others. Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Both texts are about being heard, and both use humour and short sentences. The personal essay reflects on stammering: the paradoxical hook "my name has been the hardest word I know", the phrase "kind faces trying not to look kind" and the precise "eleven seconds" reveal struggle; the ending redefines success as refusing to apologise. The speech performs confident speaking: a humorous tricolon of impossible promises, the repeated "actually" and a petition statistic win trust. The essay is reflective and personal, written to be read; the speech is persuasive and public, written to be heard.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: extract from a short story set in Valparaíso, Chile.

For twenty years my father kept the key in his wallet, behind his London bus pass. A small brass key to a blue door on Cerro Alegre.
"Why keep it?" I asked once. "The house is probably gone."
He didn't answer.
When we finally went back, the door was green. A café now. My father stood outside for a long time, then took out the key, kissed it and slipped it into the café's tip jar.
"There," he said, in Spanish. "Now it is home again."

How does the writer use the key to explore the idea of home?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The "small brass key" kept "behind his London bus pass" juxtaposes the father's two lives and symbolises exile and hope of return. His silence when asked why he keeps it shows emotion too deep to express. The fragments "the door was green. A café now." reveal the past has been replaced, yet he kisses the key and gives it to the café: an epiphany in which home is honoured by letting go. "Now it is home again" redefines home as a relationship, not a building.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text B: newspaper editorial ("Our view") on a proposed curfew for under-16s.

OUR VIEW: A CURFEW WILL NOT MAKE OUR STREETS SAFER
The council's plan to ban under-16s from the town centre after 9 p.m. may sound tough. It is also lazy.
Police figures show that youth crime in the town fell by 12 per cent last year. The problem is not that teenagers are out; it is that there is nowhere for them to go. Two youth clubs have closed since 2022.
Treat young people as suspects and they will behave like them. Fund the clubs instead.

How does the editorial argue against the curfew?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The editorial concedes the plan "may sound tough" before dismissing it as "lazy", a confident rebuttal. Statistical evidence – youth crime fell by 12 per cent and two clubs have closed – supports its argument with logos. The antithesis "The problem is not that teenagers are out; it is that there is nowhere for them to go" reframes the issue, and the closing imperative "Fund the clubs instead" offers an alternative. Opinions are presented forcefully but grounded in facts.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: final stanza of "The Mask of Anarchy" (1819) by Percy Bysshe Shelley.

Rise like Lions after slumber
In unvanquishable number—
Shake your chains to earth like dew
Which in sleep had fallen on you—
Ye are many—they are few.

Text B: poem written to be performed at a youth protest march.

They told us to wait.
We waited through three elections,
two floods and one fire season
that never really ended.

They told us to be realistic.
We are. We have done the maths.

They told us we were too young to understand.
We understand this:
you can't negotiate with a thermometer.

So we are done waiting.
Look out of your windows.
We are the weather now.

Compare how the two poems use language and form to create a voice of protest. Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Both poems address people in power through a collective voice and use repetition and memorable endings. Shelley uses imperatives ("Rise", "Shake"), similes of lions and dew, rhyming couplets and a chant-like rhythm, ending with the antithesis "Ye are many—they are few". The modern poem uses free verse and anaphora ("They told us ..."), each answered by "We", an epigram ("you can't negotiate with a thermometer") and the closing metaphor "We are the weather now". Shelley addresses the oppressed and urges them to rise; the modern poem speaks as the protesters, directly confronting adults. Contexts differ: Peterloo in 1819 and today's climate protests.

Shelley uses imperatives ("Rise", "Shake"), similes of lions and dew, rhyming couplets and a chant-like rhythm, ending with the antithesis "Ye are many—they are few". The modern poem uses free verse and anaphora ("They told us ..."), each answered by "We", an epigram ("you can't negotiate with a thermometer") and the closing metaphor "We are the weather now". Shelley addresses the oppressed and urges them to rise; the modern poem speaks as the protesters, directly confronting adults. Contexts differ: Peterloo in 1819 and today's climate protests. Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: extract from Act 2, Scene 2 of Macbeth by William Shakespeare (just after Duncan's murder).

MACBETH: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood
Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather
The multitudinous seas incarnadine,
Making the green one red.
[Re-enter LADY MACBETH]
LADY MACBETH: My hands are of your colour, but I shame
To wear a heart so white. [Knocking within] I hear a knocking
At the south entry. Retire we to our chamber.
A little water clears us of this deed.

How does Shakespeare present the Macbeths' different reactions to the murder?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: Macbeth's rhetorical question and hyperbole – his hand would "the multitudinous seas incarnadine" – show overwhelming guilt; the shift to the plain "Making the green one red" suggests collapse into simple horror. Lady Macbeth's colour imagery mocks his "heart so white" and her line "A little water clears us of this deed" shows practical confidence. The audience's later knowledge of her sleepwalking makes this dramatic irony, while the "knocking within" heightens fear of discovery.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text B: leaflet from a school eco-club in Singapore.

GO PLASTIC-FREE THIS JULY!
Did you know? Our canteen throws away about 900 plastic cups every week. That's over 30,000 a year – enough to reach the top of Marina Bay Sands if you stacked them!
What can YOU do?
• Bring a reusable bottle (free refills at the new water fountains).
• Say "no straw, please".
• Join our Thursday lunchtime clean-up.
Small changes. Big difference. Sign up at the eco-club table by Friday!

How does the leaflet persuade students that they can make a difference?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The leaflet first shocks readers with a local statistic (900 cups a week) made vivid by the Marina Bay Sands comparison, then reassures them with simple bullet-pointed imperatives. The antithesis "Small changes. Big difference." resolves the worry, and the deadline ("by Friday") creates urgency to act now.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: extract from a short story set in Cairo, Egypt.

Every evening Karim's uncle climbed to the roof to fly his pigeons. He whistled, waved a long stick with a rag tied to it, and the flock rose over the satellite dishes and the washing lines.
"Why do they always come back?" Karim asked.
His uncle shrugged. "Because this is where they are fed. Freedom is a big sky, ya Karim. But it is not dinner."
That autumn, when Karim's visa letter came, he climbed to the roof alone and stood a long time, watching the birds circle and return, circle and return.

Text B: extract from a short story set in Valparaíso, Chile.

For twenty years my father kept the key in his wallet, behind his London bus pass. A small brass key to a blue door on Cerro Alegre.
"Why keep it?" I asked once. "The house is probably gone."
He didn't answer.
When we finally went back, the door was green. A café now. My father stood outside for a long time, then took out the key, kissed it and slipped it into the café's tip jar.
"There," he said, in Spanish. "Now it is home again."

Compare how the two stories use a symbol to explore the idea of home. Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Both stories use a single object or image – pigeons and a key – to explore the pull between leaving and belonging. In the Cairo story, pigeons that always return, and the uncle's aphorism "Freedom is a big sky ... But it is not dinner", help Karim face emigration; the repetition "circle and return" ends the story with his uncertainty. In the Valparaíso story, the key "behind his London bus pass" symbolises exile; when the father gives it away, he finds an epiphany: "Now it is home again." The first story looks forward to leaving with unresolved feelings, whereas the second looks back after return and achieves resolution.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: extract from a coming-of-age novel set in a shipbuilding town in 1980s Britain.

I was twelve the summer my father stopped going to the yard, though nobody used the word "redundant" in our house. He said he was "between ships".
Every morning he still put on his work boots. He walked me to the bus stop, then kept walking – to the river, I found out later, where he stood for hours watching the empty cranes.
I thought he was the bravest man in the world. I know now that bravery and pride can look exactly the same from the height of a twelve-year-old.

How does the writer use a retrospective narrator to present the father?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The adult narrator looks back on being twelve, so the reader sees two views at once. The child accepts the euphemism "between ships" and the ritual of the work boots, but hindsight phrases ("I found out later", "I know now") reveal the father's hidden shame. The symbol of the "empty cranes" connects his loss to the collapse of the industry, and the final sentence, contrasting "bravery and pride", shows how growing up changes the narrator's understanding.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text B: speech by a 16-year-old student to a regional climate summit.

Delegates, I was born the year the reef first turned white. I am sixteen now, and I have watched it bleach four more times.
You have heard the science. You have seen the graphs. You have nodded at the statistics.
So let me ask you a simpler question: what will you tell my children when they ask what coral looked like?
We do not need more promises. We need decisions – today, in this room, before the tide goes out on our future.

How does the speaker use rhetoric to persuade her audience to act?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: She opens with ethos – her own lifetime measured in bleaching events – which makes her a credible witness. The tricolon "You have heard ... seen ... nodded" builds a rhythm of inaction ending on the dismissive "nodded". A rhetorical question about her future children creates pathos and guilt, and the antithesis "We do not need more promises. We need decisions" crystallises her demand. The closing metaphor "before the tide goes out on our future" ties urgency to the ocean itself.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: extract from a short story set in Cape Town.

The poster had been on the lamppost for three weeks: MISSING – BRUNO – REWARD. The rain had washed the dog's face into a grey smudge.
Thabo passed it every morning. Every morning he told himself it wasn't his business.
Then, on Thursday, behind the fish shop, something whined.
It was thin, and it was muddy, and one ear stood up like a question mark.
Thabo crouched. The dog looked at him. He looked at the poster. He looked at the reward. He thought about his mother's empty purse.
"Come on, Bruno," he whispered. "Let's get you home."

Text B: advertisement for a robot pet, posted on a technology website.

[Image: a silver robot puppy curled on the lap of a smiling elderly man; sunlight through a window.]
MEET PIXEL. HE NEVER NEEDS A WALK. HE NEVER FORGETS YOUR BIRTHDAY.
Powered by AI, Pixel learns your routines, reminds you of medicines and plays your favourite songs.
"I talk to him every morning," says Harold, 81, from Leeds.
Companionship, reinvented. Order today – free delivery.

Compare how the two texts present the relationship between people and animals (or animal-like companions). Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Text A presents a real, vulnerable dog ("thin ... muddy") whose rescue tests Thabo's kindness; the relationship involves responsibility and moral choice. Text B presents a robot dog as a convenient companion that "never needs a walk", selling comfort through a testimonial and a warm image. Text A uses narrative suspense and symbolism (the "question mark" ear); Text B uses persuasive anaphora and a slogan. A critical comparison: the story values care and effort, while the advert removes effort – raising questions about what companionship means.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: extract from a coming-of-age novel in which the narrator attends her brother's trial.

The courtroom was smaller than the ones on television, and quieter. Nobody shouted "Objection!".
Danny sat in a suit that belonged to our uncle. The sleeves covered his hands. He looked about nine.
When the lawyer called him "the defendant", I wanted to stand up and say his name. His name is Danny. He is scared of moths. He taught me to ride a bike.
I didn't stand up. That was the day I learned that justice is a room where you are not allowed to speak.

How does the writer present the narrator's experience of justice?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The narrator's expectations are undercut ("smaller than the ones on television"), showing justice as quiet and intimidating. Details like the borrowed suit whose "sleeves covered his hands" make Danny vulnerable, and the list of short sentences ("He is scared of moths") restores his humanity against the cold label "the defendant". The closing metaphor "justice is a room where you are not allowed to speak" shows her loss of innocence and sense of powerlessness.

TEENAGERS' APP HELPS RESCUERS REACH FLOOD FAMILIES
A free app built by three students from Lahore has helped rescue teams locate more than 400 families cut off by floods in Sindh province this week.
The app, called Pukaar ("Call"), lets users share their location and needs even with a weak signal.
"We built it in a weekend," said co-founder Hira Baig, 16. "We didn't sleep much."
Rescue coordinator Imran Shah called the app "a lifeline", but warned that thousands of people still have no phone access at all.

items.answer: The headline and lead present the app as effective, with the figure of 400 families as evidence. The quotation from 16-year-old Hira adds human interest and modesty, and the expert's metaphor "a lifeline" gives authority. The final warning keeps the report balanced and objective.

At 16, Valentina Rojas runs a weekend food stall in Lima that sells out in two hours. We asked her how.
Q: Where did you learn to cook?
A: My abuela's kitchen. She never measured anything. She'd say, 'Cook until it smells like home.'

Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: extract from Macbeth's soliloquy in Act 2, Scene 1 of Macbeth by William Shakespeare.

MACBETH: Is this a dagger which I see before me,
The handle toward my hand? Come, let me clutch thee.
I have thee not, and yet I see thee still.
Art thou not, fatal vision, sensible
To feeling as to sight? or art thou but
A dagger of the mind, a false creation,
Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain?

How does Shakespeare present Macbeth's state of mind before the murder?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: In soliloquy, Macbeth is alone with his conscience. His rhetorical questions ("Is this a dagger ...?") and apostrophe ("Come, let me clutch thee") show he is unsure what is real. The metaphor "A dagger of the mind, a false creation" suggests guilt is already distorting his perception, and "heat-oppressed brain" implies fever. Enjambement mimics his racing thoughts, building suspense just before the point of no return.

🚨SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS🚨
My cousin works at the water company and says the city's tap water will be SWITCHED OFF for 3 DAYS from Monday!!! The government doesn't want you to know.

How does the post try to persuade readers to believe and share it?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The post uses urgency ("SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS", "NOW") and fear to make readers act before thinking. Its sources are unverifiable – an anonymous "cousin" and unnamed "Doctors" – but they lend false authority. Conspiracy framing ("The government doesn't want you to know") makes denials seem like proof, and visual signals (capitals, emoji, exclamation marks) create alarm. These are classic red flags of misinformation.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: opening of a dystopian novel.

Nobody in Unity Sector had been sad for eleven years. It was against the law.
Each morning, Citizen 4471 – her friends had once called her Lena – pressed her wrist to the scanner at the factory gate. The band glowed green: Harmony Score 92. Acceptable.
Above the gate, the screen showed the Director's smiling face and the words of the day: A HAPPY CITIZEN IS A SAFE CITIZEN.
Lena smiled back. She had practised in the mirror. It hardly hurt at all.

Text B: extract from a dystopian novel in which a government department controls vocabulary.

The Ministry of Clear Speech published the new dictionary every January. This year it was thinner again.
"Protest" had become "unhelpful noise". "Prison" was now a "Calm Centre". The word "why" had been reclassified as "impolite" and was no longer taught in schools.
Jonah's little sister could not understand the old books on Grandad's shelf. "What is freedom?" she asked, sounding it out.
Jonah opened his mouth and found he did not have the words to tell her.

Compare how the two dystopian extracts show a state controlling its citizens. Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Both extracts present authoritarian states that control people through language and erase individuality. Text A uses surveillance (wrist scanners, "Harmony Score 92"), a number replacing a name and the slogan "A HAPPY CITIZEN IS A SAFE CITIZEN" to show emotions controlled. Text B shows control through vocabulary: euphemisms ("Prison" becomes "Calm Centre"), the shrinking dictionary and the banning of "why". Both end on a quiet personal moment – Lena's practised smile, Jonah lacking words – but Text A hints at resistance, whereas Text B suggests the control has already succeeded.

Choose ONE image and plan a creative piece of 400-600 words. State your form and audience, your narrator, a three-part structure and two language techniques you will use, with a reason for each.
items.answer: Model plan for Image 1 – form: story; narrator: a third-person narrator; structure: the cold – the coins don't add up – the kindness; techniques: sensory contrast of cold and warmth, dialogue, understatement. Plans for the other images must show the same elements.
items.markingKey: Model plan for Image 1 – form: story; narrator: a third-person narrator; structure: the cold – the coins don't add up – the kindness; techniques: sensory contrast of cold and warmth, dialogue, understatement. Plans for the other images must show the same elements. Marks: form and audience (1); narrator and perspective (1); coherent structure with a turning point (2); purposeful techniques (1).

items.stem:
Task 2 – Creative writing. Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A painting: a desert at night under a sky full of stars; a camel caravan's lanterns form a line of tiny lights.]
Image 2: [A photograph: a moving van parked outside a block of flats at dawn; a child presses a hand against the van's back window.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a mountain village in Nepal after an earthquake; a girl carries a school whiteboard on her back up a dusty path.]

Write a creative piece of 400-600 words inspired by ONE of the images. You may write a story, a diary entry, a letter or a speech.
items.answer: Indicative content (Image 1 example): a journey to a new life, a young guide's first crossing, or an ancient story retold; a third-person storyteller narrator; structure: departure – a test in the desert – arrival at dawn; techniques such as imagery of light and darkness, repetition, the oral-storytelling voice. Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image.

Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.
